Chapter 3: Challenging the Old Order — Why Hereditary Rule Fails
Picture this—a busy marketplace, full of noise and energy. Suddenly, a debate erupts between two neighbors. One of them passionately claims that the king and his family are meant to rule, chosen by fate and noble birth. But the other? He’s skeptical. He points out that the king’s son isn’t any wiser or kinder than the rest of us—he just had the luck of being born in a palace.
If you look around, you’ll see this same argument playing out all over. Some folks defend hereditary rule, saying tradition keeps us safe and stable, that we should trust the wisdom passed down from the past. But more and more, people are starting to notice the flaws in that logic. They’re seeing rulers who seem completely out of touch—living in luxury while ordinary people struggle just to get by. Titles and land keep passing from one generation to the next, no matter if the new ruler is really up for the job.
Imagine a teacher, feeling frustrated by the limits put on her students. She wonders why talent and hard work seem to count for so little. She sees bright kids who could do amazing things, but the system only cares about where you’re born, not what you can do. In her classroom, she encourages her students to ask questions, to dream about a world where anyone—no matter their background—has a real chance to lead and make a difference.
The cracks in hereditary rule become impossible to ignore. When someone gets power just because of their family name, it often ends up in the hands of people who aren’t prepared—or just don’t care about helping others. Decisions get made to protect privilege, not to fix real problems. And as that gap between rulers and everyone else grows, resentment and distrust start to boil over.
Some still defend the old ways, arguing that the king’s authority comes from a higher power—and that even questioning it is risky, maybe even sinful. But for a lot of people, that just doesn’t add up anymore. After all, couldn’t that same logic be used to justify almost anything, as long as it keeps those at the top in control?
So, here’s the big shift: more and more people are demanding that government should be based on consent, not inheritance. They want a real say in how they’re governed, and they insist that leaders should be chosen for their abilities—and their commitment to the common good. Those old stories about the wisdom of kings and the holiness of noble blood? They’re starting to lose their grip.
